nodes.name: log-concave distribution
nodes.statement: A distribution is \emph{log-concave} if the logarithm of its density is a concave function.
differentia: the logarithm of its density is a concave function

nodes.name: nearly-log-concave distribution
nodes.statement: A distribution with density $f(x)$ is nearly-log-concave if for any $\lambda\in[0,1]$, $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we have $f(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2)\ge e^{-0.0154}f(x_1)^\lambda f(x_2)^{1-\lambda}$~\cite{balcan2013active}.
nodes.statement_short: Density satisfies log-concavity up to the multiplicative slack $e^{-0.0154}$.

nodes.name: Geometry of s-concave distributions (informal)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then there exist \textbf{closed-form} functions $\gamma(s,m)$, $f_1(s, n)$, $f_2(s, n)$, $f_3(s, n)$, $f_4(s, n)$, and $f_5(s, n)$ such that \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]\setlength{\itemsep}{-0.1cm} \item \emph{(Weakly Closed under Marginal)} The marginal of $\mathcal{D}$ over $m$ arguments (or cumulative distribution function, CDF) is isotropic $\gamma(s,m)$-concave. (Theorems \ref{theorem: marginal}, \ref{theorem: distribution function}) \item \emph{(Lower Bound on Hyperplane Disagreement)} For any two unit vectors $u$ and $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $f_1(s, n)\theta(u,v)\le\Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}[\textup{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(v\cdot x)]$, where $\theta(u,v)$ is the angle between $u$ and $v$. (Theorem \ref{theorem: disagreement and angle}) \item \emph{(Probability of Band)} There is a function $d(s, n)$ such that for any unit vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and any $0<t\le d(s,n)$, we have $f_2(s, n)t< \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]\le f_3(s, n)t$. (Theorem \ref{theorem: probability within margin}) \item \emph{(Disagreement outside Margin)} For any absolute constant $c_1>0$ and any function $f(s,n)$, there exists a function $f_4(s,n)>0$ such that $\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\mathrm{sign}(v\cdot x)\ \text{and}\ |v\cdot x|\ge f_4(s,n)\theta(u,v)]\le c_1f(s,n)\theta(u,v)$. (Theorem \ref{theorem: disagreement outside band}) \item \emph{(Variance in 1-D Direction)} There is a function $d(s, n)$ such that for any unit vectors $u$ and $a$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\|u-a\|\le r$ and for any $0<t\le d(s, n)$, we have $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2]\le f_5(s, n)(r^2+t^2)$, where $\mathcal{D}_{u,t}$ is the conditional distribution of $\mathcal{D}$ over the set $\{x:\ |u\cdot x|\le t\}$. (Theorem \ref{theorem: 1-D variance}) \item \emph{(Tail Probability)} We have $\Pr[\|x\|>\sqrt{n}t]\le \left[1-\frac{cst}{1+ns}\right]^{(1+ns)/s}$. (Theorem \ref{theorem: tail probability}) \end{enumerate} If $s\rightarrow 0$ (i.e., the distribution is log-concave), then $\gamma(s,m)\rightarrow 0$ and the functions $f(s,n)$, $f_1(s,n)$, $f_2(s,n)$, $f_3(s,n)$, $f_4(s,n)$, $f_5(s,n)$, and $d(s,n)$ are all absolute constants.
nodes.statement_short: Isotropic $s$-concave distributions have closed-form bounds on marginal concavity, hyperplane disagreement, band probability, disagreement outside a band, 1-D variance and tail probability.

nodes.name: conditional band distribution D_{u,t}
nodes.statement: We will use capital or lower-case letters to represent random variables, $\mathcal{D}$ to represent an $s$-concave distribution, and $\mathcal{D}_{u,t}$ to represent the conditional distribution of $\mathcal{D}$ over the set $\{x:\ |u\cdot x|\le t\}$.

nodes.name: sign function
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{sign} function as $\textup{sign}(x)=+1$ if $x\ge 0$ and $-1$ otherwise.

nodes.name: beta function and gamma function
nodes.statement: We denote by $B(\alpha,\beta)=\int_0^1 t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}dt$ the beta function, and $\Gamma(\alpha)=\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t}dt$ the gamma function.

nodes.name: Euclidean norm
nodes.statement: We will consider a single norm for the vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, namely, the $2$-norm denoted by $\|x\|$.

nodes.name: measure mu of a distribution
nodes.statement: We will frequently use $\mu$ (or $\mu_f$, $\mu_\mathcal{D}$) to represent the measure of the probability distribution $\mathcal{D}$ with density function $f$.

nodes.name: ball notation
nodes.statement: The notation $\textup{\textsf{ball}}(w^*,t)$ represents the set $\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n: \|w-w^*\|\le t\}$.

nodes.name: modified addition oplus
nodes.statement: For convenience, the symbol $\oplus$ slightly differs from the ordinary addition $+$: For $f=0$ or $g=0$, $\{f^s\oplus g^s\}^{1/s}=0$; Otherwise, $\oplus$ and $+$ are the same.
nodes.statement_short: $\oplus$ is ordinary addition except that the $s$-mean is set to 0 when either argument vanishes.

nodes.name: angle between vectors
nodes.statement: For $u,v\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we define the angle between them as $\theta(u,v)$.

nodes.name: s-concave (density) function, distribution, measure
nodes.statement: A function $f$: $\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$ is $s$-concave, for $-\infty\le s\le 1$, if $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\ge (\lambda f(x)^s+(1-\lambda)f(y)^s)^{1/s}$ for all $\lambda\in[0,1]$, $\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$.\footnote{When $s\rightarrow 0$, we note that $\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}(\lambda f(x)^s+(1-\lambda)f(y)^s)^{1/s}=\exp(\lambda \log f(x)+(1-\lambda)\log f(y))$. In this case, $f(x)$ is known to be log-concave.} A probability distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is $s$-concave, if its density function is $s$-concave. A probability measure $\mu$ is $s$-concave if $\mu(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)\ge[\lambda\mu(A)^s+(1-\lambda)\mu(B)^s]^{1/s}$ for any sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is $s$-concave if $f$ at a convex combination dominates the $s$-power mean of the endpoint values; distributions and measures analogously.
nodes.label: definition: s-concavity

nodes.name: special classes of s-concave functions
nodes.statement: Special classes of $s$-concave functions include \emph{concavity} $(s=1)$, \emph{harmonic-concavity} $(s=-1)$, \emph{quasi-concavity} $(s=-\infty)$, etc.

nodes.name: hierarchy of s-concave classes
nodes.statement:
The conditions in Definition \ref{definition: s-concavity} are progressively weaker as $s$ becomes smaller: $s_1$-concave densities (distributions, measures) are $s_2$-concave if $s_1\ge s_2$. Thus one can verify~\cite{chandrasekaran2009sampling}:
$\mbox{concave }(s=1)\subsetneq \mbox{log-concave }(s=0)\subsetneq s\mbox{-concave }(s<0)\subsetneq\mbox{quasi-concave }(s=-\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: $s$-concavity weakens as $s$ decreases: concave $\subsetneq$ log-concave $\subsetneq$ $s$-concave ($s<0$) $\subsetneq$ quasi-concave.
conclusions: $s_1$-concave densities (distributions, measures) are $s_2$-concave

nodes.name: Generalized Prekopa-Leindler inequality
nodes.statement: Let $0<\lambda<1$, and $H_s$, $G_1$, and $G_2$ be non-negative integrable functions on $\mathbb{R}^m$ such that $H_s(\lambda x+(1-\lambda) y)\ge [\lambda G_1(x)^s\oplus(1-\lambda) G_2(y)^s]^{1/s}$ for every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^m$. Then $ \int_{\mathbb{R}^m}H_s(x)dx\ge \left[\lambda\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^m}G_1(x)dx\right)^\gamma+(1-\lambda)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^m}G_2(x)dx\right)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma} $ for $s\ge -1/m$, with $\gamma=s/(1+ms)$.

nodes.name: Marginal theorem for s-concave densities
nodes.statement: Let $f(x,y)$ be an $s$-concave density on a convex set $K\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ with $s\ge -\frac{1}{m}$. Denote by $K|_{\mathbb{R}^n}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m\ \mbox{s.t.}\ (x,y)\in K\}$. For every x in $K|_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, consider the section $K(x)\triangleq\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m: (x,y)\in K\}$. Then the marginal density $g(x)\triangleq\int_{K(x)}f(x,y)dy$ is $\gamma$-concave on $K|_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, where $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ms}$. Moreover, if $f(x,y)$ is isotropic, then $g(x)$ is isotropic.

nodes.name: CDF of s-concave distribution
nodes.statement: The CDF of $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\gamma$-concave, where $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ns}$ and $s\ge -\frac{1}{n}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Marginal Distribution and Cumulative Distribution Function
assumptions: $s\ge -\frac{1}{n}$
conclusions: The CDF of $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\gamma$-concave, where $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ns}$
nodes.label: theorem: distribution function

nodes.name: Tail probability of s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: Let $x$ come from an isotropic distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$ with an $s$-concave density. Then for every $t\ge 16$, we have $\Pr[\|x\|>\sqrt{n}t]\le \left[1-\frac{cst}{1+ns}\right]^{(1+ns)/s}$, where $c$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.statement_short: Isotropic $s$-concave vectors have polynomial (fat) tails: $\Pr[\|x\|>\sqrt{n}t]\le[1-cst/(1+ns)]^{(1+ns)/s}$.
assumptions: Let $x$ come from an isotropic distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$ with an $s$-concave density.
conclusions: Then for every $t\ge 16$, we have $\Pr[\|x\|>\sqrt{n}t]\le \left[1-\frac{cst}{1+ns}\right]^{(1+ns)/s}$, where $c$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.label: theorem: tail probability

nodes.name: near-tightness of the tail bound
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{theorem: tail probability} is almost tight for $s<0$.
conclusions: Theorem \ref{theorem: tail probability} is almost tight for $s<0$.

nodes.name: Proof of near-tightness of the tail bound (Pareto example)
nodes.statement: To see this, consider $X$ that is drawn from a one-dimensional Pareto distribution with density $f(x)=(-1-\frac{1}{s})^{-\frac{1}{s}}x^{\frac{1}{s}}$ $(x\ge \frac{s+1}{-s})$. It can be easily seen that $\Pr[X>t]=\left[\frac{-s}{s+1}t\right]^{\frac{s+1}{s}}$ for $t\ge \frac{s+1}{-s}$, which matches Theorem \ref{theorem: tail probability} up to an absolute constant factor.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit the one-dimensional Pareto distribution, whose tail $\Pr[X>t]$ matches the bound of Theorem 5 up to a constant.

nodes.name: Density of centroid-centered halfspaces (one-dimensional)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be drawn from a one-dimensional distribution with $s$-concave density for $-1/2\le s\le 0$. Then $\Pr(X\ge \mathbb{E} X)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$ for $\gamma=s/(1+s)$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be drawn from a one-dimensional distribution with $s$-concave density for $-1/2\le s\le 0$.
conclusions: $\Pr(X\ge \mathbb{E} X)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$ for $\gamma=s/(1+s)$.
nodes.label: lemma: halfspace probability

nodes.name: Bounds on one-dimensional isotropic s-concave density
nodes.statement: Let $g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density function and $s> -1/3$. (a) For all $x$, $g(x)\le \frac{1+s}{1+3s}$; (b) We have $g(0)\ge\sqrt{\frac{1}{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}}$, where $\gamma=\frac{s}{s+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: An isotropic 1-D $s$-concave density ($s>-1/3$) is bounded above by $(1+s)/(1+3s)$ and bounded below at 0.
assumptions: Let $g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density function and $s> -1/3$.
conclusions: (a) For all $x$, $g(x)\le \frac{1+s}{1+3s}$;
(b) We have $g(0)\ge\sqrt{\frac{1}{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}}$, where $\gamma=\frac{s}{s+1}$.
nodes.label: lemma: bound for 1 dim

nodes.name: working range of s in high dimension
nodes.statement: In the following, we will assume $-\frac{1}{2n+3}\le s\le 0$.

nodes.name: near-tightness of the working range of s
nodes.statement: Though this working range of $s$ vanishes as $n$ becomes larger, it is almost the broadest range of $s$ that we can hopefully achieve: Chandrasekaran et al.~\cite{chandrasekaran2009sampling} showed a lower bound of $s\ge -\frac{1}{n-1}$ if one require the $s$-concave distribution to have good geometric properties. In addition, we can see from Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal} that if $s<-\frac{1}{n-1}$, the marginal of an $s$-concave distribution might even not exist; Such a case does happen for certain $s$-concave distributions with $s<-\frac{1}{n-1}$, e.g., the Cauchy distribution. So our range of $s$ is almost tight up to a $1/2$ factor.
nodes.statement_short: The range $s\ge-1/(2n+3)$ is tight up to a factor 1/2, since good geometry requires $s\ge -1/(n-1)$ and marginals may fail to exist below it.

nodes.name: Density of centroid-centered halfspaces (high-dimensional)

conclusions: $\int_H f(x)dx\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$ for $\gamma=s/(1+ns)$.

nodes.name: Bounds on density of isotropic s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density. Then (a) Let $d(s,n)=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$, where $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$ and $\gamma=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}$. For any $u\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\|u\|\le d(s,n)$, we have \red{$f(u)\ge \left(\frac{\|u\|}{d}((2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1}-1)+1\right)^{1/s}f(0)$}. (b) $f(x)\le f(0)\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{1/s}$ for every $x$. (c) There exists an $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $f(x)>(4e\pi)^{-n/2}$. (d) $(4e\pi)^{-n/2}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+\frac{1}{s}}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{-\frac{1}{s}}<f(0)\le \red{(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{1/s}\frac{n\Gamma(n/2)}{2\pi^{n/2}d^n}}$. (e) \red{$f(x)\le (2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{1/s}\frac{n\Gamma(n/2)}{2\pi^{n/2}d^n}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{1/s}$} for every $x$. (f) For any line $\ell$ through the origin, $\int_{\ell} f \le \red{(2-2^{-ns})^{1/s}\frac{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform upper and lower bounds on an isotropic $s$-concave density near the origin, its maximum, and its integral over lines.
assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density.
conclusions: (a) Let $d(s,n)=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$, where $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$ and $\gamma=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}$. For any $u\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\|u\|\le d(s,n)$, we have \red{$f(u)\ge \left(\frac{\|u\|}{d}((2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1}-1)+1\right)^{1/s}f(0)$}.
(b) $f(x)\le f(0)\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{1/s}$ for every $x$.
(c) There exists an $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $f(x)>(4e\pi)^{-n/2}$.
(f) For any line $\ell$ through the origin, $\int_{\ell} f \le \red{(2-2^{-ns})^{1/s}\frac{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}}}$.
nodes.label: theorem: upper and lower bounds

nodes.name: More refined upper bound on densities
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density. Then $f(x)\le \beta_1(n,s)(1-s\beta_2(n,s)\|x\|)^{1/s}$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, where \begin{equation*} \beta_1(n,s)=\frac{(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{\frac{1}{s}}}{2\pi^{n/2}d^n}(1-s)^{-1/s}n\Gamma(n/2)\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{1/s}, \end{equation*} \begin{equation*} \beta_2(n,s)=\frac{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}}{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}(2-2^{-ns})^{-\frac{1}{s}}\frac{[(a(n,s)+(1-s)\beta_1(n,s)^s)^{1+\frac{1}{s}}-a(n,s)^{1+\frac{1}{s}}]s}{\beta_1(n,s)^s(1+s)(1-s)}, \end{equation*} $a(n,s)=(4e\pi)^{-ns/2}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{-1}$, $\gamma=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}$, $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$, and $d=(1+\gamma)^{-\frac{1}{\gamma}}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$.
nodes.statement_short: An isotropic $s$-concave density is bounded by $\beta_1(n,s)(1-s\beta_2(n,s)\|x\|)^{1/s}$ with explicit $\beta_1,\beta_2$.
assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$ be an isotropic $s$-concave density.
conclusions: Then $f(x)\le \beta_1(n,s)(1-s\beta_2(n,s)\|x\|)^{1/s}$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.label: lemma: more refined upper bound

nodes.name: Probability inside band
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Denote by $f_3(s,n)=2(1+ns)/(1+(n+2)s)$. Then for any unit vector $w$, $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]\le f_3(s,n)t. $ Moreover, if $t\le d(s,n)\triangleq\left(\frac{1+2\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)^{-\frac{1+\gamma}{\gamma}}\frac{1+3\gamma}{3+3\gamma}$ where $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$, then $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]> f_2(s,n)t, $ where $f_2(s,n)=2(2-2^{-2\gamma})^{-1/\gamma}(4e\pi)^{-1/2}\left(2\left(\frac{1+\gamma}{1+3\gamma}\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{1+2\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)^{\frac{3+3\gamma}{2\gamma}}\right)^\gamma-1\right)^{-1/\gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: The probability of a band $|w\cdot x|\le t$ is at most $f_3t$, and above $f_2t$ for $t\le d(s,n)$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
conclusions: Then for any unit vector $w$, $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]\le f_3(s,n)t.

Moreover, if $t\le d(s,n)\triangleq\left(\frac{1+2\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)^{-\frac{1+\gamma}{\gamma}}\frac{1+3\gamma}{3+3\gamma}$ where $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$, then $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]> f_2(s,n)t,
nodes.label: theorem: probability within margin

nodes.name: Probability of disagreement
nodes.statement: Assume $\mathcal{D}$ is an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for any two unit vectors $u$ and $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have $d_\mathcal{D}(u,v)=\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\textup{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(v\cdot x)]\ge f_1(s,n)\theta(u,v)$, where $f_1(s,n)=c\red{(2-2^{-3\alpha})^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}\hspace{-0.1cm}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{1+1/\alpha}\right)^{\alpha}\hspace{-0.2cm}-1\right]^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}}(1+\gamma)^{-2/\gamma}\left(\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}\right)^2$, $c$ is an absolute constant, $\alpha=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$, $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$, $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ns}$.
nodes.statement_short: Disagreement probability of two halfspaces is at least $f_1(s,n)$ times their angle.
assumptions: Assume $\mathcal{D}$ is an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
conclusions: Then for any two unit vectors $u$ and $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have $d_\mathcal{D}(u,v)=\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\textup{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(v\cdot x)]\ge f_1(s,n)\theta(u,v)$
nodes.label: theorem: disagreement and angle

nodes.name: Margin Based Active Learning under S-Concave Distributions
nodes.statement: \footnotesize \caption{Margin Based Active Learning under S-Concave Distributions} \begin{algorithmic} \STATE {\bfseries Input:} Parameters $b_k$, $\tau_k$, $r_k$, $m_k$, $\kappa$, and $T$ as in Theorem \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning adversarial noise}. \STATE {\bfseries 1:} Draw $m_1$ examples from $\mathcal{D}$, label them and put them into $W$. \STATE {\bfseries 2:} \ \ \textbf{For} $k=1,2,...,T$ \STATE {\bfseries 3:} \quad Find $v_k\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}(w_{k-1},r_k)$ to approximately minimize the hinge loss over $W$ s.t. $\|v_k\|\le 1$:\\ \qquad\ $\ell_{\tau_k}\le \min_{w\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}(w_{k-1},r_k)\cap \textup{\textsf{ball}}(0,1)} \ell_{\tau_k}(w,W)+\kappa/8$. \STATE {\bfseries 4:} \quad Normalize $v_k$, yielding $w_k=\frac{v_k}{\|v_k\|}$; Clear the working set $W$. \STATE {\bfseries 5:} \quad \textbf{While} $m_{k+1}$ additional data points are not labeled \STATE {\bfseries 6:} \quad \quad Draw sample $x$ from $\mathcal{D}$. \STATE {\bfseries 7:} \quad \quad \textbf{If} $|w_k\cdot x|\ge b_k$, reject $x$; \textbf{else} ask for label of $x$ and put into $W$. \STATE {\bfseries Output:} Hypothesis $w_T$. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Localized active learning: each round minimizes hinge loss in a ball around the previous separator, then queries labels only in a shrinking band.
input: Parameters $b_k$, $\tau_k$, $r_k$, $m_k$, $\kappa$, and $T$ as in Theorem \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning adversarial noise}.
nodes.label: algorithm: margin based active learning adversarial noise

nodes.name: Disagreement outside band
nodes.statement: Let $u$ and $v$ be two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and assume that $\theta(u,v)=\theta<\pi/2$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution. Then for any absolute constant $c_1>0$ and any function $f_1(s,n)>0$, there exists a function $f_4(s,n)>0$ such that $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\mathrm{sign}(v\cdot x)\ \text{and}\ |v\cdot x|\ge f_4(s,n)\theta]\le c_1f_1(s,n)\theta, $ where $f_4(s,n)=\frac{4\beta_1(2,\alpha)B(-1/\alpha-3,3)}{-c_1f_1(s,n)\alpha^3\beta_2(2,\alpha)^3}$, $B(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the beta function, $\alpha=s/(1+(n-2)s)$, $\beta_1(2,\alpha)$ and $\beta_2(2,\alpha)$ are given by Lemma \ref{lemma: more refined upper bound}.
nodes.statement_short: Most disagreement between two close halfspaces lies inside a band of width $f_4\theta$ around one of them.
assumptions: Let $u$ and $v$ be two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and assume that $\theta(u,v)=\theta<\pi/2$.
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution.
conclusions: Then for any absolute constant $c_1>0$ and any function $f_1(s,n)>0$, there exists a function $f_4(s,n)>0$ such that $ \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(u\cdot x)\not=\mathrm{sign}(v\cdot x)\ \text{and}\ |v\cdot x|\ge f_4(s,n)\theta]\le c_1f_1(s,n)\theta,
nodes.label: theorem: disagreement outside band

nodes.name: 1-D variance
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{D}$ is isotropic $s$-concave. For $d$ given by Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a), there is an absolute $C_0$ such that for all $0<t\le d$ and for all $a$ such that $\|u-a\|\le r$ and $\|a\|\le 1$, $ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2]\le f_5(s,n)(r^2+t^2), $ where $f_5(s,n)=16+C_0\frac{8\beta_1(2,\eta)B(-1/\eta-3,2)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)^3(\eta+1)\eta^2}$, $(\beta_1(2,\eta), \beta_2(2,\eta))$ and $f_2(s,n)$ are given by Lemma \ref{lemma: more refined upper bound} and Theorem \ref{theorem: probability within margin}, and $\eta=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Within a band around $u$, the second moment along any direction $a$ close to $u$ is $O(f_5(r^2+t^2))$.
assumptions: Assume that $\mathcal{D}$ is isotropic $s$-concave.
for all $0<t\le d$ and for all $a$ such that $\|u-a\|\le r$ and $\|a\|\le 1$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2]\le f_5(s,n)(r^2+t^2),

nodes.name: Margin-based active learning, realizable case
nodes.statement: In the realizable case, let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for $0<\epsilon<1/4$, $\delta>0$, and absolute constants $c$, there is an algorithm (see the supplementary material) that runs in $T=\lceil\log \frac{1}{c\epsilon}\rceil$ iterations, requires $m_k\hspace{-0.1cm}=\hspace{-0.1cm}O\hspace{-0.1cm}\left(\frac{f_3\min\{2^{-k}f_4f_1^{-1},d\}}{2^{-k}}\left(n\log \frac{f_3\min\{2^{-k}f_4f_1^{-1},d\}}{2^{-k}}\hspace{-0.1cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}\log \frac{1+s-k}{\delta}\right)\hspace{-0.1cm}\right)$ labels in the $k$-th round, and outputs a linear separator of error at most $\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. In particular, when $s\rightarrow 0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), we have $m_k=O\left(n+\log(\frac{1+s-k}{\delta})\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: In the realizable case, margin-based active learning reaches error $\epsilon$ in $\lceil\log(1/c\epsilon)\rceil$ rounds with per-round labels depending on $f_1,f_3,f_4$.
assumptions: In the realizable case, let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
for $0<\epsilon<1/4$, $\delta>0$, and absolute constants $c$
conclusions: there is an algorithm (see the supplementary material) that runs in $T=\lceil\log \frac{1}{c\epsilon}\rceil$ iterations, requires $m_k\hspace{-0.1cm}=\hspace{-0.1cm}O\hspace{-0.1cm}\left(\frac{f_3\min\{2^{-k}f_4f_1^{-1},d\}}{2^{-k}}\left(n\log \frac{f_3\min\{2^{-k}f_4f_1^{-1},d\}}{2^{-k}}\hspace{-0.1cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}\log \frac{1+s-k}{\delta}\right)\hspace{-0.1cm}\right)$ labels in the $k$-th round, and outputs a linear separator of error at most $\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
In particular, when $s\rightarrow 0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), we have $m_k=O\left(n+\log(\frac{1+s-k}{\delta})\right)$.
nodes.label: theorem: margin-based active learning realizable case

nodes.name: exponential improvement in the realizable case
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning realizable case}, we see that the algorithm of margin-based active learning under $s$-concave distributions works almost as well as the log-concave distributions in the resizable case, improving exponentially w.r.t. the variable $1/\epsilon$ over passive learning algorithms.

nodes.name: adversarial noise model
nodes.statement: In the adversarial noise model, an adversary can choose any distribution $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ over $\mathbb{R}^n\times \{+1,-1\}$ such that the marginal $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $s$-concave but an $\eta$ fraction of labels can be flipped adversarially.
nodes.statement_short: Labels come from an adversarial joint distribution whose $x$-marginal is $s$-concave, with an $\eta$ fraction of labels flipped.

nodes.name: Margin-based active learning with adversarial noise
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution in $\mathbb{R}^n$ over $x$ and the label $y$ obey the adversarial noise model. If the rate $\eta$ of adversarial noise satisfies $\eta<c_0\epsilon$ for some absolute constant $c_0$, then for $0<\epsilon<1/4$, $\delta>0$, and an absolute constant $c$, Algorithm \ref{algorithm: margin based active learning adversarial noise} runs in $T=\lceil\log \frac{1}{c\epsilon}\rceil$ iterations, outputs a linear separator $w_T$ such that $\Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}[\textup{sign}(w_T\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x)]\le\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. The label complexity in the $k$-th round is $m_k=O\left( \frac{[b_{k-1}s+\tau_k(1+ns)[1-(\delta/(\sqrt{n}(k+k^2)))^{s/(1+ns)}]+\tau_ks]^2}{\kappa^2\tau_k^2s^2}n\left(n+\log \frac{k+k^2}{\delta}\right)\right)$, where $\kappa=\max\left\{\frac{f_3\tau_k}{f_2\min\{b_{k-1},d\}},\frac{b_{k-1}\sqrt{f_5}}{\tau_k\sqrt{f_2}}\right\}$, $\tau_k=\Theta\left(f_1^{-2}f_2^{-1/2}f_3f_4^2f_5^{1/2}2^{-(k-1)}\right)$, $b_k=\min\{\Theta(2^{-k}f_4f_1^{-1}),d\}$. In particular, if $s\rightarrow 0$, $m_k=O\left(n\log(\frac{n}{\epsilon\delta})(n+\log(\frac{k}{\delta}))\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under adversarial noise $\eta<c_0\epsilon$, Algorithm 1 outputs an $\epsilon$-accurate halfspace with explicit per-round label complexity.

If the rate $\eta$ of adversarial noise satisfies $\eta<c_0\epsilon$ for some absolute constant $c_0$

The label complexity in the $k$-th round is $m_k=O\left( \frac{[b_{k-1}s+\tau_k(1+ns)[1-(\delta/(\sqrt{n}(k+k^2)))^{s/(1+ns)}]+\tau_ks]^2}{\kappa^2\tau_k^2s^2}n\left(n+\log \frac{k+k^2}{\delta}\right)\right)$

nodes.name: exponential improvement under adversarial noise
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning adversarial noise}, the label complexity of margin-based active learning improves exponentially over that of passive learning w.r.t. $1/\epsilon$ even under fat-tailed $s$-concave distributions and challenging adversarial noise model.

nodes.statement: Let the Alexander capacity $\mbox{cap}_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}=\frac{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}}(\text{DIS}(\textup{\textsf{ball}}_{\mathcal{D}}(w^*,r)))}{r}$.

nodes.name: disagreement coefficient
nodes.statement: The disagreement coefficient is defined as $\Theta_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(\epsilon)=\sup_{r\ge\epsilon}[\text{cap}_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(r)]$.

nodes.name: Disagreement coefficient under s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$. For any $w^*$ and $r>0$, the disagreement coefficient is $\Theta_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(\epsilon)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}(1+ns)^2}{s(1+(n+2)s)f_1(s,n)}(1-\epsilon^{\frac{s}{1+ns}})\right)$. In particular, when $s\rightarrow0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), $\Theta_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(\epsilon)=O(\sqrt{n}\log(1/\epsilon))$.
nodes.statement_short: The disagreement coefficient of halfspaces under isotropic $s$-concave distributions is $O(\sqrt{n}(1+ns)^2(1-\epsilon^{s/(1+ns)})/(s(1+(n+2)s)f_1))$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an isotropic $s$-concave distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$.
For any $w^*$ and $r>0$
conclusions: the disagreement coefficient is $\Theta_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(\epsilon)=O\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}(1+ns)^2}{s(1+(n+2)s)f_1(s,n)}(1-\epsilon^{\frac{s}{1+ns}})\right)$.
In particular, when $s\rightarrow0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), $\Theta_{w^*,\mathcal{D}}(\epsilon)=O(\sqrt{n}\log(1/\epsilon))$.
nodes.label: theorem: disagreement coefficient

nodes.name: comparison of disagreement coefficient bounds
nodes.statement: Our bounds on the disagreement coefficient match the best known results for the much less general case of log-concave distributions~\cite{balcan2013active}; Furthermore, they apply to the $s$-concave case where we allow arbitrary number of discontinuities, a case not captured by \cite{friedman2009active}. The result immediately implies concrete bounds on the label complexity of disagreement-based active learning algorithms, e.g., CAL~\cite{cohn1994improving} and $A^2$~\cite{balcan2009agnostic}.

nodes.name: label complexity of agnostic disagreement-based active learning
nodes.statement:
For instance, by composing it with the result from \cite{dasgupta2007general}, we obtain a bound of
$$\widetilde O\left(n^{3/2}\frac{(1+ns)^2}{s(1+(n+2)s)f(s)}(1-\epsilon^{s/(1+ns)})\left(\log^2 \frac{1}{\epsilon}+\frac{OPT^2}{\epsilon^2}\right)\right)$$
for \emph{agnostic} active learning under an isotropic $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Namely, it suffices to output a halfspace with error at most $OPT+\epsilon$, where $OPT=\min_{w}\textup{\textsf{err}}_\mathcal{D}(w)$.
nodes.statement_short: Combining the disagreement coefficient bound with Dasgupta-Hsu-Monteleoni gives an agnostic label complexity bound reaching error $OPT+\epsilon$.
conclusions: we obtain a bound of $$\widetilde O\left(n^{3/2}\frac{(1+ns)^2}{s(1+(n+2)s)f(s)}(1-\epsilon^{s/(1+ns)})\left(\log^2 \frac{1}{\epsilon}+\frac{OPT^2}{\epsilon^2}\right)\right)$$ for \emph{agnostic} active learning under an isotropic $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Baum's algorithm under s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: In the PAC realizable case, there is an algorithm (see the supplementary material) that outputs a hypothesis $h$ of error at most $\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ under isotropic $s$-concave distributions. The label complexity is $M(\epsilon/2,\delta/4,n^2)+\max\{2m_2/\epsilon,(2/\epsilon^2)\log(4/\delta)\}$, where $M(\epsilon,\delta,m)$ is defined by $M(\epsilon,\delta,n)=O\left(\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon}+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$, $m_2=M(\max\{\delta/(4eKm_1),\epsilon/2\},\delta/4,n)$, $d=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$, $K=\beta_1(3,\kappa)\frac{B(-1/\kappa-3,3)}{(-\kappa\beta_2(3,\kappa))^3}\frac{3+1/\kappa}{h(\kappa)d^{3+1/\kappa}}$, $\beta=\frac{\kappa}{1+2\kappa}$, $\gamma=\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}$, $\kappa=\frac{s}{1+(n-3)s}$, and $h(\kappa)=\left(\frac{1}{d}((2-2^{-4\kappa})^{-1}-1)+1\right)^{\frac{1}{\kappa}}(4e\pi)^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1\hspace{-0.1cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{2+\frac{1}{\kappa}}\right)^{\kappa}\hspace{-0.2cm}-\hspace{-0.1cm}1\right]^{-1/\kappa}$. In particular, if $s\rightarrow 0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), $K$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.statement_short: Baum's algorithm PAC-learns intersections of two halfspaces under isotropic $s$-concave distributions with explicit label complexity.
assumptions: In the PAC realizable case
conclusions: there is an algorithm (see the supplementary material) that outputs a hypothesis $h$ of error at most $\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ under isotropic $s$-concave distributions.
The label complexity is $M(\epsilon/2,\delta/4,n^2)+\max\{2m_2/\epsilon,(2/\epsilon^2)\log(4/\delta)\}$
In particular, if $s\rightarrow 0$ (a.k.a. log-concave), $K$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.label: theorem: Baum's algorithm

nodes.name: Lower bounds for learning halfspaces under s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: For a fixed value $-\frac{1}{2n+3}\le s\le 0$ we have: (a) For any $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose covariance matrix is of full rank, the sample complexity of learning origin-centered linear separators under $\mathcal{D}$ in the passive learning scenario is $\Omega\left(nf_1(s,n)/\epsilon\right)$; (b) The label complexity of active learning of linear separators under $s$-concave distributions is $\Omega\left(n\log\left(f_1(s,n)/\epsilon\right)\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Passive learning needs $\Omega(nf_1/\epsilon)$ samples and active learning $\Omega(n\log(f_1/\epsilon))$ labels.
assumptions: For a fixed value $-\frac{1}{2n+3}\le s\le 0$
conclusions: (a) For any $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose covariance matrix is of full rank, the sample complexity of learning origin-centered linear separators under $\mathcal{D}$ in the passive learning scenario is $\Omega\left(nf_1(s,n)/\epsilon\right)$;
(b) The label complexity of active learning of linear separators under $s$-concave distributions is $\Omega\left(n\log\left(f_1(s,n)/\epsilon\right)\right)$.
nodes.label: theorem: lower bounds of learning halfspace

nodes.name: lower bounds apply to all s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: If the covariance matrix of $\mathcal{D}$ is not of full rank, then the intrinsic dimension is less than $d$. So our lower bounds essentially apply to all $s$-concave distributions.

nodes.name: exponential improvement of active over passive learning
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{theorem: lower bounds of learning halfspace}, it is possible to have an exponential improvement of label complexity w.r.t. $1/\epsilon$ over passive learning by active sampling, even though the underlying distribution is a fat-tailed $s$-concave distribution. This observation is captured by Theorems \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning realizable case} and \ref{theorem: margin-based active learning adversarial noise}.

nodes.name: Proof of Marginal theorem for s-concave densities
nodes.statement: The proof that $g(x)$ is isotropic is standard~\cite{lovasz2007geometry}. We now prove the first part. Let $x_1$, $x_2$ be any two points. Define $g_i(y)=f(x_i,y)$ for $i=1,2$. So the functions $g_i(y)$ is defined on $K(x_i)$, $i=1,2$. Now let $x=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2$ for $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and define $h_s(y)=f(x,y)$ on $K(x)$. Notice that for any $y_i\in K(x_i)$, $i=1,2$, $y=\lambda y_1+(1-\lambda)y_2\in K(x)$. To see this, by the convexity of the set $K$, the point $(x,y)=\lambda(x_1,y_1)+(1-\lambda)(x_2,y_2)$ belongs to $K$. So $y\in K(x)$, i.e., $\lambda K(x_1)+(1-\lambda)K(x_2)\subseteq K(x)$. Using the $s$-concavity of $f(x,y)$, we have $f(x,y)=f(\lambda(x_1,y_1)+(1-\lambda)(x_2,y_2))\ge \left[\lambda f(x_1,y_1)^s+(1-\lambda)f(x_2,y_2)^s\right]^{1/s}$, which implies that $h_s(y)=h_s(\lambda y_1+(1-\lambda)y_2)\ge \left[\lambda g_1(y_1)^s+(1-\lambda)g_2(y_2)^s\right]^{1/s}$. Denote by $I_{(\cdot)}$ the indicator function. So $h_s(\lambda y_1+(1-\lambda)y_2)I_{K(x)}(y)\ge \left[\lambda (g_1(y_1)I_{K(x_1)}(y_1))^s\oplus(1-\lambda)(g_2(y_2)I_{K(x_2)}(y_2))^s\right]^{1/s}$. Set $H_s(y)\hspace{-0.1cm}=\hspace{-0.1cm}h_s(\lambda y_1\hspace{-0.1cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}(1\hspace{-0.1cm}-\hspace{-0.1cm}\lambda)y_2)I_{K(x)}$, $G_1(y_1)\hspace{-0.1cm}=\hspace{-0.1cm}g_1(y_1)I_{K(x_1)}$, $G_2(y_1)=g_2(y_1)I_{K(x_2)}$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: generalized prekopa-leindler inequality}, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} g(x)&=\hspace{-0.1cm}\int_{\mathbb{R}^m}H_s(y)dy=\hspace{-0.1cm}\int_{\mathbb{R}^m}h_s(y)I_{K(x)}(y)dy\ge \hspace{-0.1cm}\left[(1\hspace{-0.1cm}-\hspace{-0.1cm}\lambda)\hspace{-0.1cm}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\hspace{-0.2cm}G_1(y)dy\right)^\gamma\hspace{-0.2cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}\lambda\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\hspace{-0.2cm}G_2(y)dy\right)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}\\ &=\left[(1-\lambda)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x_1,y_1)I_{K(x_1)}(y_1)dy_1\right)^\gamma+\lambda\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x_2,y_2)I_{K(x_2)}(y_2)dy_2\right)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}\\ &=\left[(1-\lambda)g(x_1)^\gamma+\lambda g(x_2)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}, \end{split} \end{equation*} where $\gamma=s/(1+ms)$. Namely, the marginal function $g(x)$ is $\gamma$-concave.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the generalized Prekopa-Leindler inequality (Theorem 2) to the sections $K(x_1)$, $K(x_2)$, $K(x)$ using convexity of $K$ and $s$-concavity of $f$.

nodes.statement_short: Isotropy of the marginal is standard.

nodes.name: Generalized Brunn-Minkowski inequality
nodes.statement: The density function $f(x)$ is $s$-concave for $s\ge -1/n$ where $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, if and only if the corresponding probability measure $\mu$ is $\gamma$-concave for $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ns}$, namely, $\mu(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)\ge \left[\lambda\mu(A)^\gamma+(1-\lambda)\mu(B)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}$, for any $A,B\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, where $\mu(A)=\int_A f(x)dx$.
nodes.statement_short: A density is $s$-concave ($s\ge-1/n$) iff its measure is $s/(1+ns)$-concave.
assumptions: for $s\ge -1/n$ where $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$
conclusions: The density function $f(x)$ is $s$-concave

if and only if the corresponding probability measure $\mu$ is $\gamma$-concave for $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+ns}$, namely, $\mu(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)\ge \left[\lambda\mu(A)^\gamma+(1-\lambda)\mu(B)^\gamma\right]^{1/\gamma}$, for any $A,B\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, where $\mu(A)=\int_A f(x)dx$.
nodes.label: lemma: generalized brunn-minkowski inequality

nodes.name: Proof of CDF of s-concave distribution
nodes.statement: Denote by $F(x)$ the CDF. Applying Lemma \ref{lemma: generalized brunn-minkowski inequality} to the set $A=\{x: x\le x_1\}$ and $B=\{x: x\le x_2\}$ and taking into account that $F(x_1)=\mu(A)$, $F(x_2)=\mu(B)$, and $F(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2)=\mu(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)$, we have the result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the generalized Brunn-Minkowski lemma to the lower orthants $\{x\le x_1\}$ and $\{x\le x_2\}$.

nodes.name: Large deviations for kappa-concave measures
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a Borel function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $m$ be a median for $|f|$ w.r.t. a $\kappa$-concave measure $\mu$, where $\kappa<0$. Then for every $t>1$ such that $4\delta_f(\frac{1}{t})\le 1$, we have $ \mu[|f|>mt]\le\left[1-\frac{c\kappa}{\delta_f(\frac{1}{t})}\right]^{1/\kappa}, $ where $c$ is a constant, $ \delta_f(\epsilon)=\sup_{x,y} \mbox{mes}\{t\in(0,1):|f(tx+(1-t)y)|\le\epsilon|f(x)|\},\ 0\le\epsilon\le 1, $ and mes stands for the Lebesgue measure.
nodes.statement_short: For a $\kappa$-concave measure ($\kappa<0$), $|f|$ exceeds $t$ times its median with polynomially small probability controlled by $\delta_f(1/t)$.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a Borel function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $m$ be a median for $|f|$ w.r.t. a $\kappa$-concave measure $\mu$, where $\kappa<0$.
for every $t>1$ such that $4\delta_f(\frac{1}{t})\le 1$
conclusions: \mu[|f|>mt]\le\left[1-\frac{c\kappa}{\delta_f(\frac{1}{t})}\right]^{1/\kappa},
nodes.label: lemma: tail probability median

nodes.name: Proof of Tail probability of s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: Set function $f(x)$ in Lemma \ref{lemma: tail probability median} as $\|x\|$. Bobkov~\cite{bobkov2007large} claimed that $\delta_f(\epsilon)\le2\epsilon$. Also, Lemma \ref{lemma: generalized brunn-minkowski inequality} implies that the probability measure is $\kappa=\frac{s}{1+ns}$-concave. By the definition of the median $m$, the Markov inequality, and the Jensen inequality, we have $\frac{1}{2}=\Pr[\|x\|\ge m]\le \frac{\mathbb{E}\|x\|}{m}\le\frac{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|x\|^2}}{m}=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{m}$, where the last equality is due to the isotropicity assumption. So by Lemma \ref{lemma: tail probability median}, we have that for every $t\ge 8$, $\Pr[\|x\|>2\sqrt{n}t]\le \Pr[\|x\|>mt]\le \left[1-cst/(1+ns)\right]^{(1+ns)/s}$. Replacing $t$ with $t/2$, the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Bobkov's large-deviation lemma to $f(x)=\|x\|$, bounding the median by $2\sqrt{n}$ via Markov and Jensen.

nodes.name: Set up Bobkov's lemma
nodes.statement: Set function $f(x)$ in Lemma \ref{lemma: tail probability median} as $\|x\|$. Bobkov~\cite{bobkov2007large} claimed that $\delta_f(\epsilon)\le2\epsilon$. Also, Lemma \ref{lemma: generalized brunn-minkowski inequality} implies that the probability measure is $\kappa=\frac{s}{1+ns}$-concave.

nodes.name: Bound the median
nodes.statement:
By the definition of the median $m$, the Markov inequality, and the Jensen inequality, we have

where the last equality is due to the isotropicity assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Markov and Jensen give $m\le 2\sqrt{n}$ under isotropy.

So by Lemma \ref{lemma: tail probability median}, we have that for every $t\ge 8$,
$\Pr[\|x\|>2\sqrt{n}t]\le \Pr[\|x\|>mt]\le \left[1-cst/(1+ns)\right]^{(1+ns)/s}$.
Replacing $t$ with $t/2$, the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Bobkov's bound and rescale $t$.

nodes.name: Proof of Density of centroid-centered halfspaces (one-dimensional)
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mathbb{E} X=0$ and $|X|\le K$. The general case then follows by translation transformation and approximating a general distribution with $s$-concave density by such bounded distributions. Let $G(x)=\Pr(X\le x)$ be the CDF of the $s$-concave density. We first prove that $\Pr(X\le \mathbb{E} X)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: distribution function}, $G(x)$ is $\gamma$-concave, monotone increasing such that $G(x)=0$ for $x\le -K$ and $G(x)=1$ for $x\ge K$, where $-1\le \gamma=\frac{s}{1+s}\le0$. Notice that the assumption of centroid 0 implies that $ \int_{-K}^KxG'(x)dx=0, $ which equivalently means $ \int_{-K}^KG(x)dx=K $ by integration by parts. Our goal is to prove that $G(0)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$. The function $G^\gamma$ is concave for $\gamma<0$. Thus it lies above its tangent at $0$. This means that $G(x)\le G(0)(1+\gamma cx)^\frac{1}{\gamma}$, where $c=G'(0)/G(0)>0$. We now set $K$ large enough so that $1/c<K$. Then \begin{equation*} G(x)\le \begin{cases} G(0)(1+\gamma cx)^\frac{1}{\gamma}, & \mbox{if}\ x\le 1/c,\\ 1, & \mbox{if}\ x> 1/c. \end{cases} \end{equation*} So \begin{equation*} \begin{split} K&=\int_{-K}^KG(x)dx\\ &\le \int_{-K}^{1/c}G(0)(1+\gamma cx)^\frac{1}{\gamma}dx+\int_{1/c}^K1dx\\ &=\frac{G(0)}{c(\gamma+1)}[(1+\gamma)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}+1}-(1-\gamma cK)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}+1}]+K-\frac{1}{c}\\ &\le\frac{G(0)(1+\gamma)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}}}{c}+K-\frac{1}{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} which implies that $G(0)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$ as claimed. Replacing $X$ with $Y=-X$, we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Tangent-line argument on the $\gamma$-concave CDF $G$: bound $\int G=K$ above to force $G(0)\ge(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$.

nodes.name: Reduction to bounded centered case
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mathbb{E} X=0$ and $|X|\le K$. The general case then follows by translation transformation and approximating a general distribution with $s$-concave density by such bounded distributions.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG centered and bounded; general case by translation and approximation.

nodes.name: CDF is gamma-concave
nodes.statement: Let $G(x)=\Pr(X\le x)$ be the CDF of the $s$-concave density. We first prove that $\Pr(X\le \mathbb{E} X)\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: distribution function}, $G(x)$ is $\gamma$-concave, monotone increasing such that $G(x)=0$ for $x\le -K$ and $G(x)=1$ for $x\ge K$, where $-1\le \gamma=\frac{s}{1+s}\le0$.
nodes.statement_short: The CDF $G$ is $\gamma$-concave by Theorem 4.

nodes.name: Centroid condition

Notice that the assumption of centroid 0 implies that
$
\int_{-K}^KxG'(x)dx=0,
$
which equivalently means
$
\int_{-K}^KG(x)dx=K
$

nodes.statement_short: Centroid zero gives $\int_{-K}^K G=K$ by integration by parts.

nodes.name: Tangent bound
nodes.statement: The function $G^\gamma$ is concave for $\gamma<0$. Thus it lies above its tangent at $0$. This means that $G(x)\le G(0)(1+\gamma cx)^\frac{1}{\gamma}$, where $c=G'(0)/G(0)>0$.

nodes.name: Integrate the bound
nodes.statement_short: Integrating the piecewise bound yields $G(0)\ge(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}$.

nodes.name: Moment properties of s-concave functions
nodes.statement: Let $g:\mathbb{R}_+\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an integrable function. Define $M_n(g)=\int_0^\infty t^ng(t)dt$, and suppose it exists. Then (a) The sequence $\{M_n(g): n=0,1,...\}$ is log-convex, which means $\log M_n(g)$ is convex w.r.t. variable $n$, or equivalently $M_n(g)M_{n+2}(g)\ge M_{n+1}(g)^2$ for any $n\in N$. (b) If $g$ is monotone decreasing, then the sequence defined by \begin{equation*} M_n'(g)= \begin{cases} nM_{n-1}(g), & \mbox{if}\ n>0,\\ g(0), & \mbox{if}\ n=0, \end{cases} \end{equation*} is log-convex. (c) If $g$ is $s$-concave ($s>-1/(n+1)$), then the sequence $T_n(g)\triangleq M_n(g)/B(-1/s-n-1,n+1)$ is log-concave, which means $\log T_n(g)$ is concave w.r.t. $n$, or equivalently $T_n(g)T_{n+2}(g)\le T_{n+1}(g)^2$ for any $n\in N$. (d) If $g$ is $s$-concave, then $g(0)M_1(g)\le M_0(g)^2\frac{1+s}{1+2s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Moment sequences of integrable functions are log-convex; normalized by beta functions they are log-concave for $s$-concave $g$, with $g(0)M_1\le M_0^2(1+s)/(1+2s)$.
assumptions: Let $g:\mathbb{R}_+\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ be an integrable function. Define $M_n(g)=\int_0^\infty t^ng(t)dt$, and suppose it exists.
conclusions: (a) The sequence $\{M_n(g): n=0,1,...\}$ is log-convex, which means $\log M_n(g)$ is convex w.r.t. variable $n$, or equivalently $M_n(g)M_{n+2}(g)\ge M_{n+1}(g)^2$ for any $n\in N$.

(b) If $g$ is monotone decreasing, then the sequence defined by \begin{equation*} M_n'(g)= \begin{cases} nM_{n-1}(g), & \mbox{if}\ n>0,\\ g(0), & \mbox{if}\ n=0, \end{cases} \end{equation*} is log-convex.

(c) If $g$ is $s$-concave ($s>-1/(n+1)$), then the sequence $T_n(g)\triangleq M_n(g)/B(-1/s-n-1,n+1)$ is log-concave, which means $\log T_n(g)$ is concave w.r.t. $n$, or equivalently $T_n(g)T_{n+2}(g)\le T_{n+1}(g)^2$ for any $n\in N$.
(d) If $g$ is $s$-concave, then $g(0)M_1(g)\le M_0(g)^2\frac{1+s}{1+2s}$.
nodes.label: lemma: moment property

nodes.name: Proof of Moment properties of s-concave functions
nodes.statement: The proofs of Parts (a) and (b) are from \cite{lovasz2007geometry}. (c) The intuition behind the proof is to choose a baseline $s$-concave function $h$ which is at the ``boundary" between the family of $s$-concave function and that of the non $s$-concave function. We show that $h$ satisfies the equation \begin{equation} T_n(h)T_{n+2}(h)=T_{n+1}^2(h). \end{equation} Then by the facts that $h$ is at the ``boundary" and $g$ is any $s$-concave function, we have \begin{equation} T_{n+1}(h)\le T_{n+1}(g). \end{equation} The conclusion follows from \eqref{equ: equality for special function} and \eqref{equ: comparison}, and from our choice of $h$ such that $T_n(h)=T_n(g)$ and $T_{n+2}(h)=T_{n+2}(g)$, by adjusting the slope and intercept of the linear function. Formally, let $h(t)=\beta(1+\gamma t)^{1/s}$ be the above-mentioned baseline $s$-concave function ($\beta,\gamma>0$) such that \begin{equation*} M_n(h)=M_n(g)\ \ \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \ \ M_{n+2}(h)=M_{n+2}(g) \end{equation*} (This holds because there are two parameters $\beta,\gamma$ and two equations). That means \begin{equation*} \int_0^\infty t^n(h(t)-g(t))dt=0\ \ \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \ \ \int_0^\infty t^{n+2}(h(t)-g(t))dt=0. \end{equation*} Then it follows that the graph of $h$ must intersect the graph of $g$ at least twice. Since $g$ is $s$-concave, which implies the uni-modality, the graphs of $h$ and $g$ intersect exactly at two points $0\le a<b$. Moreover, $h\le g$ in the interval $[a,b]$ and $h\ge g$ outside the interval. That is to say, $(t-a)(t-b)$ has the same sign as $h-g$. Thus \begin{equation*} \int_0^{\infty} (t-a)(t-b)t^n(h(t)-g(t))dt\ge 0. \end{equation*} Namely, \begin{equation*} 0=\int_0^{\infty}t^{n+2}(h(t)-g(t))dt+ab\int_0^{\infty}t^n(h(t)-g(t))dt\ge (a+b)\int_0^\infty t^{n+1}(h(t)-g(t))dt. \end{equation*} This implies that \begin{equation*} M_{n+1}(h)=\int_0^{\infty}t^{n+1}h(t)dt\le\int_0^\infty t^{n+1}g(t)dt=M_{n+1}(g). \end{equation*} Since \begin{equation*} M_n(h)=\int_0^\infty t^n\beta(1+\gamma t)^{1/s}dt=B(-1/s-n-1,n+1)\frac{\beta}{\gamma^{n+1}} \end{equation*} for $s>-1/(n+1)$, we have \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \frac{M_n(g)}{B(-1/s-n-1,n+1)}\frac{M_{n+2}(g)}{B(-1/s-n-3,n+3)}&=\frac{M_n(h)}{B(-1/s-n-1,n+1)}\frac{M_{n+2}(h)}{B(-1/s-n-3,n+3)}\\ &=\frac{\beta}{\gamma^{n+1}}\cdot \frac{\beta}{\gamma^{n+3}}\\ &=\left(\frac{M_{n+1}(h)}{B(-1/s-n-2,n+2)}\right)^2\\ &\le \left(\frac{M_{n+1}(g)}{B(-1/s-n-2,n+2)}\right)^2, \end{split} \end{equation*} as desired. (d) The proof is almost the same as that of Part (c). Let $h(t)=\beta(1+\gamma t)^{1/s}$ be an $s$-concave function ($\beta,\gamma>0$) such that \begin{equation*} h(0)=g(0)\ \ \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \ \ M_1(h)=M_1(g). \end{equation*} So the graphs of $h$ and $g$ intersect exactly at two points $0$ and $a>0$, and hence \begin{equation*} \int_0^{\infty}t(t-a)t^{-1}(h(t)-g(t))dt\ge 0. \end{equation*} That means \begin{equation*} 0=\int_0^{\infty}t(h(t)-g(t))dt\ge a\int_0^{\infty}(h(t)-g(t))dt, \end{equation*} or equivalently, \begin{equation*} M_0(h)\le M_0(g). \end{equation*} Note that $h(0)M_1(h)=M_0(h)^2\frac{1+s}{1+2s}$ by \eqref{equ: integral}. Then the conclusion follows by the fact \begin{equation*} g(0)M_1(g)=h(0)M_1(h)=M_0(h)^2\frac{1+s}{1+2s}\le M_0(g)^2\frac{1+s}{1+2s}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of Bounds on one-dimensional isotropic s-concave density
nodes.statement: (a) Let $z$ be the maximum point of function $g$. Intuitively, if the value of the function $g$ evaluated at $z$ is too large, the corresponding distribution has a small deviation from $z$ (Second part of the proof below). However, the moment property of Lemma \ref{lemma: moment property} restricts that the second moment cannot be too small (First part of the proof below), which leads to a contradiction. Formally, suppose that $g(z)>\frac{1+s}{1+3s}$. Define \begin{equation*} M_i=\int_z^{\infty}(x-z)^ig(x)dx,\ \ \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \ \ N_i=\int_{-\infty}^z(z-x)^ig(x)dx. \end{equation*} By the isotropicity of function $g$, we have \begin{equation*} M_0+N_0=1,\ \ \ \ N_1-M_1=z,\ \ \ \ M_2+N_2=1+z^2. \end{equation*} Thus \begin{equation*} \begin{split} M_2+N_2&=(M_0+N_0)^2+(M_1-N_1)^2\\ &=(M_0-M_1)^2+(N_0-N_1)^2+2(M_0N_0-M_1N_1)+2(M_0M_1+N_0N_1)\\ &\ge 2(M_0M_1+N_0N_1), \end{split} \end{equation*} where the last inequality holds since, by Lemma \ref{lemma: moment property} (d), we have $M_1\le\frac{M_0^2}{g(z)}\frac{1+s}{1+2s}\le M_0^2\le M_0$ and $N_1\le\frac{N_0^2}{g(z)}\frac{1+s}{1+2s}\le N_0^2\le N_0$. On the other hand, by Lemma \ref{lemma: moment property} (c) (d), \begin{equation*} M_2\le \frac{2M_1^2}{M_0}\frac{1+2s}{1+3s}\le \frac{2M_1M_0}{g(z)}\frac{1+s}{1+3s}<2M_1M_0, \end{equation*} and similarly, $N_2<2N_1N_0$. That means \begin{equation*} M_2+N_2<2(M_0M_1+N_0N_1), \end{equation*} and we obtain a contradiction. (b) The proof is by Lemma \ref{lemma: moment property} (b) which lower bounds $g(0)$ by the second order moment of $g$, which is $1$ according to isotropicity. Specifically, without lose of generality, assume that $g(x)$ is monotone decreasing for $x\ge 0$ (otherwise consider $g(-x)$, since function $g$ is uni-modal). Define $g_0$ as the restriction of $g$ to the non-negative semi-line. Then by Lemma \ref{lemma: moment property} (b), we have \begin{equation*} M_1'(g_0)^3\le M_0'(g_0)^2M_3'(g_0), \end{equation*} which implies \begin{equation*} g(0)\ge \sqrt{\frac{M_0(g_0)^3}{3M_2(g_0)}}. \end{equation*} Note that $M_2(g_0)\le M_2(g)=1$, and by Lemma \ref{lemma: halfspace probability}, \begin{equation*} M_0(g_0)=\int_0^\infty g(t)dt=\Pr[X\ge \mathbb{E} X]\ge (1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}. \end{equation*} Thus we have \begin{equation*} g(0)\ge \sqrt{\frac{1}{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}}, \end{equation*} where $\gamma=s/(1+s)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Bounds on density of isotropic s-concave distributions
nodes.statement: (a) Formally, suppose that the conclusion does not hold true, i.e., there is a point $u$ such that $\|u\|=t\le d$ and \red{$f(u)<\left(\frac{t}{d}((2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1}-1)+1\right)^{1/s}f(0)$}. Define $v=\frac{d}{t}u$ and note that $0\le \frac{t}{d}\le 1$. Therefore, by the $s$-concavity of $f$, we have \begin{equation*} f(u)=f\left(\frac{t}{d}v+\left(1-\frac{t}{d}\right)0\right)\ge \left[\frac{t}{d}f(v)^s+\left(1-\frac{t}{d}\right)f(0)^s\right]^{1/s}, \end{equation*} which together with $f(u)<\left(\frac{t}{d}((2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1}-1)+1\right)^{1/s}f(0)$ implies \red{$f(v)<(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1/s}f(0)$}. Let $H$ be a hyperplane supporting the convex set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: f(x)\ge f(v)\}$ through the point $v$ (the convexity follows from the $s$-concavity of $f$). Define an orthogonal coordinate system in which the hyperplane is parallel to coordinate plane so that it can be represented as $x_1=a$ for some $0<a\le d$. Thus \red{$f(x)<(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1/s}f(0)$} for any $x$ such that $x_1\ge a$. We will prove that this implies that the 1-dimensional marginal is not flat. Denote by $g$ the first marginal of the $n$-dimensional function $f$. Then $g$ is isotropic and $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$-concave by Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}, and $g(x)\le \frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}$ for all $x$ by Lemma \ref{lemma: bound for 1 dim} (a). We prove that \begin{equation*} g(2b)<\frac{g(b)}{4} \end{equation*} for any $b\ge a$, which means that the 1-dimensional function is not flat. To see this, by the $s$-concavity of function $f$, we have that, for every $x$ such that $x_1\ge a$, \begin{equation*} f(2x)^s\ge 2f(x)^s-f(0)^s>2^{-(n+1)s}f(x)^s. \end{equation*} Namely, $f(2x)< 2^{-(n+1)}f(x)$. Hence \begin{equation*} g(2b)=\int_{(x_1=2b)}f(x)dx_2...dx_n< 2^{-(n+1)}2^{n-1}\int_{(x_1=b)}f(x)dx_2...dx_n=\frac{g(b)}{4}. \end{equation*} So \begin{equation*} \int_a^\infty g(y)dy=\int_a^{2a} g(y)dy+\int_{2a}^\infty g(y)dy< \int_a^{2a} g(y)dy+\frac{1}{2}\int_a^{\infty} g(y)dy. \end{equation*} Namely, by Lemma \ref{lemma: bound for 1 dim} (a), \begin{equation*} \int_a^{\infty} g(y)dy< 2\int_a^{2a} g(y)dy\le 2a\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}. \end{equation*} So \begin{equation*} \int_0^{\infty} g(y)dy=\int_0^a g(y)dy+\int_a^{\infty} g(y)dy< 3a\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\le 3d\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}, \end{equation*} which leads to a contradiction with Lemma \ref{lemma: halfspace probability}. (b) If $f(w)\le f(0)$ for every $w$, then the conclusion holds true. Otherwise, let $w$ be the point such that $f(w)> f(0)$. Let $H_0$ be the hyperplane through $0$ which supports the convex set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\ge f(0)\}$. By defining an orthogonal system, we may set $H_0$ as the hyperplane $x_1=0$, and so $f(x)\le f(0)$ for any $x$ such that $x_1=0$. Define $g$, which is a $\beta=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$-concave function, as the first marginal of function $f$. Denote by $H_t$ the hyperplane $x_1=t$. Without loss of generality, we assume that $w\in H_b$ with $b>0$. Let $x$ be any point on $H_0$ and $x'$ be the intersection between line segment $[x,w]$ and $H_{b/2}$. Then by the $s$-concavity of $f$ and $f(x)\le f(0)$ for $x\in H_0$, we have \begin{equation*} f(x')\ge \left[\frac{1}{2}f(x)^s+\frac{1}{2}f(w)^s\right]^{1/s}\ge\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1/s}f(x)\left[1+\left(\frac{f(w)}{f(0)}\right)^{s}\right]^{1/s}. \end{equation*} Thus \begin{equation*} g(b/2)=\int_{(x_1=b/2)}f(x)dx_2...dx_n\ge\frac{1}{2^{n-1+1/s}}\left[1+\left(\frac{f(w)}{f(0)}\right)^{s}\right]^{1/s}g(0). \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{lemma: bound for 1 dim} (a) (b), we have \begin{equation*} \frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\ge g(b/2)\ge \frac{1}{2^{n-1+1/s}}\left[1+\left(\frac{f(w)}{f(0)}\right)^{s}\right]^{1/s}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}}, \end{equation*} where $\gamma=\beta/(1+\beta)$. Note that $s\ge -\frac{1}{2n+3}$ implies $\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}2^{n-1+1/s}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}<1$. So \begin{equation*} f(w)\le f(0)\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{1/s}. \end{equation*} (c) The proof of Part (c) follows from \cite{lovasz2007geometry}. (d) The proof of lower bound follows from Parts (b) and (c). For the upper bound, by Part (a), we have \begin{equation*} 1=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)dx\ge \int_{\|x\|\le d}f(x)dx\ge \red{d^n \text{vol}(B_{n-1})(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{-1/s}f(0),} \end{equation*} where $\text{vol}(B_{n-1})$ represents the volume of $n-1$-dimensional unit ball. So \begin{equation*} f(0)\le \red{\frac{(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{1/s}}{d^n\text{vol}(B_{n-1})}=(2-2^{-(n+1)s})^{1/s}\frac{n\Gamma(n/2)}{2\pi^{n/2}d^n}.} \end{equation*} (e) The proof of (e) follows from Parts (b) and (d). (f) Define an orthogonal coordinate system in which $\ell$ is the $x_n$-axis. Let $h$ be the marginal of function $f$ over first $n-1$ variables, namely, \begin{equation*} h(x_1,...,x_{n-1})=\int f(x_1,...,x_{n-1},x_n)dx_n. \end{equation*} Then \begin{equation*} \int_{\ell} f=h(0)\le \red{(2-2^{-ns})^{1/s}\frac{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}}.} \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: We first note that when $\|x\|\le 1/\beta_2$, $\beta_1(1-s\beta_2\|x\|)^{1/s}\ge \beta_1(1-s)^{1/s}\ge f(x)$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (e). We will prove that \begin{equation*} \int_\ell f > \red{(2-2^{-ns})^{1/s}\frac{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}},} \end{equation*} which leads to a contradiction with Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (f). Let $x$ be the convex combination of points $0$ and $v$, i.e., $x=(1-\|x\|/\|v\|)0+(\|x\|/\|v\|)v$, where $0\le \|x\|\le\|v\|$. Then by the $s$-concavity of $f$ and Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (d), \begin{equation*} \begin{split} f(x)&\ge \left[\left(1-\frac{\|x\|}{\|v\|}\right)f(0)^s+\frac{\|x\|}{\|v\|}f(v)^s\right]^{1/s}\\&> \red{\left[f(0)^s+\frac{\|x\|}{\|v\|}f(v)^s\right]^{1/s}}\\ &> \left[f(0)^s+\frac{\|x\|}{\|v\|}\beta_1^s-s\beta_1^s\beta_2\|x\|\right]^{1/s}\\&>\left[f(0)^s+(1-s)\beta_1^s\beta_2\|x\|\right]^{1/s}\\ &> \left\{(4e\pi)^{-ns/2}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}-1\right]^{-1}+(1-s)\beta_1^s\beta_2\red{\|x\|}\right\}^{1/s}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Thus \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \int_\ell f\ge \int_{[0,v]}f&=\int_0^{\|v\|} \hspace{-0.2cm}\left\{(4e\pi)^{-ns/2}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}\hspace{-0.2cm}-\hspace{-0.1cm}1\right]^{-1}\hspace{-0.3cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}(1-s)\beta_1^s\beta_2r\right\}^{1/s}\hspace{-0.2cm} dr\\ &>\int_0^{1/\beta_2} \hspace{-0.2cm}\left\{(4e\pi)^{-ns/2}\left[\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1+3\beta}\sqrt{3(1+\gamma)^{3/\gamma}}2^{n-1+1/s}\right)^{s}\hspace{-0.2cm}-\hspace{-0.1cm}1\right]^{-1}\hspace{-0.3cm}+\hspace{-0.1cm}(1-s)\beta_1^s\beta_2r\right\}^{1/s}\hspace{-0.2cm} dr\\ &\ge \red{(2-2^{-ns})^{1/s}\frac{(n-1)\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}d^{n-1}}.} \end{split} \end{equation*} So the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Near the origin use Theorem 9(e); far away, contradiction: $s$-concavity along $[0,v]$ makes the line integral exceed Theorem 9(f).

nodes.name: Small norm
nodes.statement: We first note that when $\|x\|\le 1/\beta_2$, $\beta_1(1-s\beta_2\|x\|)^{1/s}\ge \beta_1(1-s)^{1/s}\ge f(x)$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (e). So the conclusion holds.
nodes.statement_short: For $\|x\|\le1/\beta_2$ the bound follows from Theorem 9(e).

nodes.name: Assume violation
nodes.statement_short: Assume a violating $v$; aim to contradict Theorem 9(f).

nodes.name: Lower bound along segment
nodes.statement_short: s-concavity and Theorem 9(d) lower bound $f$ on $[0,v]$.

nodes.name: Integrate along the line
nodes.statement_short: Integrating gives a line integral above the Theorem 9(f) bound.

nodes.name: Upper bound on band probability (restated)
nodes.statement: \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]\le f_3(s,n)t.

nodes.name: Lower bound on band probability (restated)
nodes.statement: \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]> f_2(s,n)t,

nodes.name: Proof of Probability inside band
nodes.statement: Define an orthogonal coordinate system in which $w$ is an axis. Then the distribution of $w\cdot x$ is equal to the first marginal of the distribution $\mathcal{D}$, with isotropic $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$-concave density $g$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}. According to the upper bound given by Lemma \ref{lemma: bound for 1 dim} (a), \begin{equation*} \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]=\int_{-t}^t g(x)dx\le \frac{1+\gamma}{1+3\gamma}\int_{-t}^t dx=2\frac{1+ns}{1+(n+2)s}t. \end{equation*} We now prove the later part of the theorem by a similar argument. By Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a) (d), for 1-dimensional $\gamma$-concave density $f(u)$ and $\|u\|\le d$, we have \begin{equation*} \begin{split} f(u)&\ge (2-2^{-2\gamma})^{-1/\gamma}f(0)\\ &>(2-2^{-2\gamma})^{-1/\gamma}(4e\pi)^{-1/2}\left(2\left(\frac{1+\gamma}{1+3\gamma}\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{1+2\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)^{\frac{3+3\gamma}{2\gamma}}\right)^\gamma-1\right)^{-1/\gamma}\\ &\triangleq \frac{f_2(s,n)}{2}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Therefore, \begin{equation*} \Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[|w\cdot x|\le t]=\int_{-t}^t g(x)dx> \frac{f_2(s,n)}{2}\int_{-t}^t dx=f_2(s,n)t. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Project onto $w$ (marginal is $\gamma$-concave by Theorem 3) and integrate the 1-D density bounds of Lemma 7(a) and Theorem 9(a),(d) over $[-t,t]$.

nodes.name: Reduce to 1-D marginal
nodes.statement: Define an orthogonal coordinate system in which $w$ is an axis. Then the distribution of $w\cdot x$ is equal to the first marginal of the distribution $\mathcal{D}$, with isotropic $\gamma=\frac{s}{1+(n-1)s}$-concave density $g$ by Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}.
nodes.statement_short: The law of $w\cdot x$ is the first marginal, $\gamma$-concave by Theorem 3.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the density upper bound of Lemma 7(a).

nodes.name: Density lower bound
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 9(a),(d) lower bound the 1-D density near 0 by $f_2/2$.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement_short: Integrate over $[-t,t]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Probability of disagreement
nodes.statement: Consider the 2-dimensional space spanned by vectors $u$ and $v$, and let $\mathcal{D}_2$ be the marginal of distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over that space. Since $d_{\mathcal{D}}(u,v)=d_{\mathcal{D}_2}(u',v')$, where $u'$ and $v'$ are projection of $u$ and $v$, respectively, we only need to focus on the marginal distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$, which has an $\alpha$-concave density according to Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}, and is isotropic according to Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}. Let $A$ be the disagreement region of $u$ and $v$ intersected with the ball of radius $d=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a) and (d), $ d_{\mathcal{D}}(u,v)=d_{\mathcal{D}_2}(u',v')\ge \mbox{vol}(A)\inf_{x\in A} p(x)\ge f_1(s,n)\theta(u',v')=f_1(s,n)\theta(u,v), $ where $p(x)$ is the density of distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the 2-D marginal on span$(u,v)$ and lower bound the density on the disagreement wedge within radius $d$.

nodes.name: Reduce to 2-D
nodes.statement: Consider the 2-dimensional space spanned by vectors $u$ and $v$, and let $\mathcal{D}_2$ be the marginal of distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over that space. Since $d_{\mathcal{D}}(u,v)=d_{\mathcal{D}_2}(u',v')$, where $u'$ and $v'$ are projection of $u$ and $v$, respectively, we only need to focus on the marginal distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$, which has an $\alpha$-concave density according to Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}, and is isotropic according to Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal}.
nodes.statement_short: Disagreement depends only on the 2-D marginal, $\alpha$-concave and isotropic.

nodes.name: Volume times density
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be the disagreement region of $u$ and $v$ intersected with the ball of radius $d=(1+\gamma)^{-1/\gamma}\frac{1+3\beta}{3+3\beta}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. By Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a) and (d),
$
d_{\mathcal{D}}(u,v)=d_{\mathcal{D}_2}(u',v')\ge \mbox{vol}(A)\inf_{x\in A} p(x)\ge f_1(s,n)\theta(u',v')=f_1(s,n)\theta(u,v),
$
where $p(x)$ is the density of distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound by area of the wedge times the infimum density (Theorem 9).

nodes.name: Proof of Disagreement outside band
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be the event that we want to bound. Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal} implies that, without loss of generality, we can focus on the case when $n=2$. Then the projected distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$ has an $\alpha$-concave density, where $\alpha=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$. We first claim that each member $x$ of $E$ satisfies $\|x\|\ge f_4$. To see this, without loss of generality, we assume that $v\cdot x$ is positive. Then for any $x\in E$, $u\cdot x<0$, i.e., $\theta(u,x)\ge \pi/2$. Hence $\theta(x,v)\ge \theta(u,x)-\theta(u,v)\ge \pi/2-\theta$. Since $|v\cdot x|\ge f_4\theta$ implies $\|x\|\cos\theta(v,x)\ge f_4\theta$, we must have $\|x\|\cos(\pi/2-\theta)\ge f_4\theta$, namely, $\|x\|\ge f_4\theta/\sin(\theta)\ge f_4$. Let $\textup{\textsf{ball}}(r)$ denote the ball of radius $r$ centered at the origin. This implies that \begin{equation*} \Pr[E]=\sum_{i=1}^\infty \Pr[E\cap (\textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)-\textup{\textsf{ball}}(if_4))]. \end{equation*} Denote by $f(x_1,x_2)$ the $\alpha$-concave density function of $\mathcal{D}_2$. For any term $i\ge 1$, by Lemma \ref{lemma: more refined upper bound}, we have \begin{equation*} \begin{split} &\ \ \ \ \Pr[E\cap (\textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)-\textup{\textsf{ball}}(if_4))]\\ &=\int_{(x_1,x_2)\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)-\textup{\textsf{ball}}(if_4)}1_E(x_1,x_2)f(x_1,x_2)dx_1dx_2\\ &\le \int_{(x_1,x_2)\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)-\textup{\textsf{ball}}(if_4)}1_E(x_1,x_2)\beta_1(2,\alpha)(1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)\|x\|)^{1/\alpha}dx_1dx_2\\ &\le \beta_1(2,\alpha)\left(1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)if_4\right)^{1/\alpha}\int_{(x_1,x_2)\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)-\textup{\textsf{ball}}(if_4)}1_E(x_1,x_2)dx_1dx_2\\ &\le \beta_1(2,\alpha)\left(1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)if_4\right)^{1/\alpha}\int_{(x_1,x_2)\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)}1_E(x_1,x_2)dx_1dx_2. \end{split} \end{equation*} Denote by $B_1$ the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Notice that \begin{equation*} \int_{(x_1,x_2)\in \textup{\textsf{ball}}((i+1)f_4)}1_E(x_1,x_2)dx_1dx_2\le \text{vol}(B_1)(i+1)^2f_4^2\theta/\pi. \end{equation*} Thus \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \Pr[E]&\le\sum_{i=1}^\infty \beta_1(2,\alpha)\left(1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)if_4\right)^{1/\alpha}\text{vol}(B_1)(i+1)^2f_4^2\theta/\pi\\ &\le \frac{4f_4^2}{\pi}\text{vol}(B_1)\beta_1(2,\alpha)\theta\sum_{i=1}^\infty (1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)if_4)^{1/\alpha}i^2\\ &\le \frac{4f_4^2}{\pi}\text{vol}(B_1)\beta_1(2,\alpha)\theta\int_0^\infty x^2(1-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)f_4x)^{1/\alpha}dx\\ &=\frac{4f_4^2}{\pi}\text{vol}(B_1)\beta_1(2,\alpha) \frac{B(-1/\alpha-3,3)}{(-\alpha\beta_2(2,\alpha)f_4)^3}\times \theta\\ &=4\beta_1(2,\alpha) \frac{B(-1/\alpha-3,3)}{-\alpha^3\beta_2(2,\alpha)^3f_4}\times \theta. \end{split} \end{equation*} Choosing $f_4(s,n)=\frac{4\beta_1(2,\alpha)B(-1/\alpha-3,3)}{-c_1f_1(s,n)\alpha^3\beta_2(2,\alpha)^3}$, the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $n=2$; points of the event have norm $\ge f_4$; sum the refined density bound (Lemma 10) over annuli and compare with a beta integral.

nodes.name: Reduce to two dimensions
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be the event that we want to bound. Theorem \ref{theorem: marginal} implies that, without loss of generality, we can focus on the case when $n=2$. Then the projected distribution $\mathcal{D}_2$ has an $\alpha$-concave density, where $\alpha=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3 WLOG $n=2$ with an $\alpha$-concave density.

nodes.name: Claim: large norm
nodes.statement: We first claim that each member $x$ of $E$ satisfies $\|x\|\ge f_4$. To see this, without loss of generality, we assume that $v\cdot x$ is positive. Then for any $x\in E$, $u\cdot x<0$, i.e., $\theta(u,x)\ge \pi/2$. Hence $\theta(x,v)\ge \theta(u,x)-\theta(u,v)\ge \pi/2-\theta$. Since $|v\cdot x|\ge f_4\theta$ implies $\|x\|\cos\theta(v,x)\ge f_4\theta$, we must have $\|x\|\cos(\pi/2-\theta)\ge f_4\theta$, namely, $\|x\|\ge f_4\theta/\sin(\theta)\ge f_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Every point of $E$ has $\|x\|\ge f_4$.

nodes.name: Angle bound
nodes.statement: To see this, without loss of generality, we assume that $v\cdot x$ is positive. Then for any $x\in E$, $u\cdot x<0$, i.e., $\theta(u,x)\ge \pi/2$. Hence $\theta(x,v)\ge \theta(u,x)-\theta(u,v)\ge \pi/2-\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of $E$ make angle $\ge\pi/2-\theta$ with $v$.

nodes.name: Norm bound
nodes.statement: Since $|v\cdot x|\ge f_4\theta$ implies $\|x\|\cos\theta(v,x)\ge f_4\theta$, we must have $\|x\|\cos(\pi/2-\theta)\ge f_4\theta$, namely, $\|x\|\ge f_4\theta/\sin(\theta)\ge f_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\|x\|\ge f_4\theta/\sin\theta\ge f_4$.

nodes.name: Annuli decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\Pr[E]$ over annuli of width $f_4$.

nodes.name: Refined density bound
nodes.statement_short: Bound each annulus term using Lemma 10.

nodes.name: Wedge area
nodes.statement_short: The area of $E$ in a ball is a $\theta/\pi$ fraction.

nodes.name: Sum to a beta integral
nodes.statement_short: Sum over annuli and bound by a beta-function integral.

nodes.name: Choose f_4
nodes.statement: Choosing $f_4(s,n)=\frac{4\beta_1(2,\alpha)B(-1/\alpha-3,3)}{-c_1f_1(s,n)\alpha^3\beta_2(2,\alpha)^3}$, the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $f_4$ to make the bound $c_1f_1\theta$.

nodes.name: Probability outside margin in the band
nodes.statement: For $d$ given by Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a), there exist such that for any isotropic $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$, for any $a$ such that $\|a\|\le 1$ and $\|u-a\|\le r$, for any $0<t\le d$, and for any $K\ge 4$, we have \begin{equation*} \Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2})\le \frac{4\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-c\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)K\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{t}{r}\right)^2}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}, \end{equation*} where $\beta_1(2,\eta)$, $\beta_2(2,\eta)$, and $Q(\gamma)$, are given by Lemma \ref{lemma: more refined upper bound} and Theorem \ref{theorem: probability within margin}, respectively, $\eta=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$, and $c$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on a band around $u$, $|a\cdot x|$ exceeds $K\sqrt{r^2+t^2}$ with probability decaying polynomially in $K$.
assumptions: For $d$ given by Theorem \ref{theorem: upper and lower bounds} (a), there exist such that for any isotropic $s$-concave distribution $\mathcal{D}$, for any $a$ such that $\|a\|\le 1$ and $\|u-a\|\le r$, for any $0<t\le d$, and for any $K\ge 4$
conclusions: \Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2})\le \frac{4\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-c\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)K\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{t}{r}\right)^2}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}},
nodes.label: lemma: probability of outside of margin

nodes.name: Proof of Probability outside margin in the band
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $u=(1,0,...,0)$. Let $a'=(0,a_2,...,a_d)$ and $X=(x_1,x_2,...,x_d)\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}$. So the probability that we want to bound is \begin{equation*} \Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2})=\frac{\Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2},\ |x_1|\le t)}{\Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(|x_1|\le t)}. \end{equation*} According to Theorem \ref{theorem: probability within margin}, there is a function $Q(\gamma)$ such that the denominator obeys the following lower bound when $t\le d$: \begin{equation*} \Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}}(|x_1|\le t)\ge f_2(s,n)t. \end{equation*} So the remainder of the proof is to bound the numerator. Note that we have \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2},\ |x_1|\le t)&\le \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(|a'\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2}-t,\ |x_1|\le t)\\ &\le \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(|a'\cdot x|> (K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2},\ |x_1|\le t). \end{split} \end{equation*} Denote by $a''=\frac{a'}{\|a'\|}$. Define random variable $Y$ as $a''\cdot x$ and $Z$ as $x_1$ where $x\sim\mathcal{D}$. Then the joint distribution of $Y$ and $Z$ is isotropic $\beta$-concave with $\eta=\frac{s}{1+(n-2)s}$. Let $f(y,z)$ be the density of such a distribution. Then we can bound the numerator by \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 4\Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}}(a'\cdot x>(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2},\ 0\le x_1\le t)&=4\Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}}(a''\cdot x>\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|},\ 0\le x_1\le t)\\ &\le 4\int_0^t\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty f(y,z) dydz. \end{split} \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{lemma: more refined upper bound}, we note that \begin{equation*} f(y,z)\le \beta_1(2,\eta)(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\sqrt{y^2+z^2})^{1/\eta}. \end{equation*} Therefore, the numerator can be upper bounded by \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\quad \ 4\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_0^t\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\sqrt{y^2+z^2})^{1/\eta} dydz\\ &\le 4\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_0^t\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)y)^{1/\eta} dydz\\ &=4t\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)y)^{1/\eta} dy\\ &=\frac{4t\beta_1(2,\eta)}{\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}. \end{split} \end{equation} Note that $\|a'\|\le r$. Finally, we have \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \Pr_{X\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}(|a\cdot x|> K\sqrt{r^2+t^2})&\le \frac{4\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{r}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}\\ &\le \frac{4\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-c\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{K\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{r}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}, \end{split} \end{equation*} for an absolute constant $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the conditional probability as a ratio; lower bound the denominator by Theorem 11 and upper bound the numerator by integrating the refined density bound of Lemma 10 on the 2-D marginal.

nodes.name: Ratio form
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $u=e_1$; write the conditional probability as a ratio.

nodes.name: Denominator bound
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 11 lower bounds the band probability by $f_2t$.

nodes.name: Reduce numerator
nodes.statement_short: Replace $a$ by its orthogonal part $a'$.

nodes.name: 2-D joint density
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $Y=a''\cdot x$, $Z=x_1$ with $\eta$-concave joint density.

nodes.name: Integrate refined bound
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 10 bounds the numerator by an explicit integral.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement_short: Use $\|a'\|\le r$ to conclude.

nodes.name: Upper bound on the numerator
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\quad \ 4\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_0^t\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\sqrt{y^2+z^2})^{1/\eta} dydz\\ &\le 4\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_0^t\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)y)^{1/\eta} dydz\\ &=4t\beta_1(2,\eta)\int_{\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}}^\infty (1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)y)^{1/\eta} dy\\ &=\frac{4t\beta_1(2,\eta)}{\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\left(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{(K-1)\sqrt{r^2+t^2}}{\|a'\|}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}. \end{split}

nodes.name: Proof of 1-D variance
nodes.statement: Denote by $z=\sqrt{r^2+t^2}$. Then we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2]&=\int_0^\infty \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2\ge z]dz\\ &\le 16z^2+\int_{16z^2}^\infty \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal{D}_{u,t}}[(a\cdot x)^2\ge z]dz\\ &\le 16z^2+\frac{4\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\int_0^\infty\left(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{c\sqrt{z}}{r}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}dz\\ &=16z^2+\frac{8\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}\int_0^\infty y\left(1-\eta\beta_2(2,\eta)\frac{cy}{r}\right)^{\frac{\eta+1}{\eta}}dy\\ &=16z^2+\frac{8\beta_1(2,\eta)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)}\frac{1}{\eta+1}C_0B(-1/\eta-3,2)\frac{r^2}{\eta^2\beta_2(2,\eta)^2}\\ &=\left(16+C_0\frac{8\beta_1(2,\eta)B(-1/\eta-3,2)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)^3(\eta+1)\eta^2}\right)r^2+16t^2\\ &\le \left(16+C_0\frac{8\beta_1(2,\eta)B(-1/\eta-3,2)}{f_2(s,n)\beta_2(2,\eta)^3(\eta+1)\eta^2}\right)(r^2+t^2), \end{split} \end{equation} where $c$, $C_0$ are absolute constants.
nodes.statement_short: Layer-cake formula for the second moment, splitting at $16z^2$ and bounding the tail with Lemma 23.

nodes.name: Second moment bound in the band

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Assume now that the claim is true for $k-1$. We now consider the $k$th iteration. Denote by $S_{k-1}=\{x: |w_{k-1}\cdot x|\le b_{k-1}\}$ and $\bar S_{k-1}=\{x: |w_{k-1}\cdot x|> b_{k-1}\}$. By the induction hypothesis, with probability at least $1-\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{i<k-1}\frac{1}{(1+s-i)^2}$, any $w$ that is consistent with $W(k-1)$, including $w_{k-1}$, has error at most $c2^{-(k-1)}$. For such a hypothesis $w$ and $w_{k-1}$, by Theorem \ref{theorem: disagreement and angle}, we have $\theta(w,w^*)\le cf_1^{-1}2^{-(k-1)}$ and $\theta(w_{k-1},w^*)\le cf_1^{-1}2^{-(k-1)}$. Thus $\theta(w_{k-1},w)\le \theta(w_{k-1},w^*)+\theta(w^*,w)\le 4cf_1^{-1} 2^{-k}$. So by Theorem \ref{theorem: disagreement outside band}, there is a choice of band width $b_{k-1}=\min\{\Theta(f_4f_1^{-1}2^{-k}),d\}$ such that $\Pr(\textup{sign}(w\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w_{k-1}\cdot x),x\in \bar S_{k-1})\le \frac{c2^{-k}}{4}$ and $\Pr[\textup{sign}(w_{k-1}\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x),x\in \bar S_{k-1}]\le \frac{c2^{-k}}{4}$. Therefore,
$\Pr[\textup{sign}(w\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x), x\in\bar S_{k-1}]\le \frac{c2^{-k}}{2}$.

We now consider the case when $x\in S_{k-1}$. By Algorithm \ref{algorithm: margin based active learning realizable case}, we label $m_k$ data points in $S_{k-1}$ at the $(k-1)$th iteration. So according to the VC theory (Theorem \ref{theorem: vc theory}), with probability at least $1-\delta/(4(1+s-k)^2)$, for all $w$ that is consistent with the examples in $W(k)$,
$
\textup{\textsf{err}}(w|S_{k-1})=\Pr[\textup{sign}(w\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x)|x\in S_{k-1}]\le \frac{c2^{-k}}{2b_{k-1}f_3}
$.
Finally, note that Theorem \ref{theorem: probability within margin} implies that $\Pr(S_{k-1})\le f_3b_{k-1}$. So we have
$\textup{\textsf{err}}(w)=\Pr[\textup{sign}(w\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x), x\in\bar S_{k-1}]+\Pr[\textup{sign}(w\cdot x)\not=\textup{sign}(w^*\cdot x), x\in S_{k-1}]\le \frac{c2^{-k}}{2}+\frac{c2^{-k}}{2b_{k-1}f_3}\times f_3b_{k-1}=c2^{-k}$.
The proof is completed.
